title: Monitoring: System, Data & Model
interviewAnswer: Monitor system health such as failures and latency, data quality/drift, and model quality when ground truth becomes available. Version models so a degraded release can be rolled back.
why: Models can fail while servers look healthy, and servers can fail while offline model metrics remain excellent. You need separate monitoring layers.
intuition: System monitoring asks “is the service running?” Data monitoring asks “does input still look valid?” Model monitoring asks “are predictions still useful?”
deepDive: Track errors, availability, latency and resource use; validate schemas/ranges and distribution changes; measure model quality when ground truth arrives; slice metrics by important cohorts. Drift is a diagnostic signal, not an automatic retrain trigger.
math: Examples: p95 latency, error rate, null-rate change, PSI/KS-style drift statistics, delayed precision/recall.
code:
# Simple monitoring shape
log(request_id, model_version, latency_ms, input_schema_ok)
metrics.observe('prediction_latency_ms', latency_ms)
# Later, join predictions to ground truth and compute quality by model_version.
commonMistakes: Monitoring only CPU/GPU and ignoring model/data quality.
Retraining automatically whenever any drift detector fires.
No model version in prediction logs, making rollback diagnosis hard.
followUps: What if labels arrive after 30 days?
How would you monitor a generative model?
production: Create alerts around user-facing SLOs and hard data contracts. Keep a stable previous model version ready for rollback; use canary/shadow releases for higher-risk changes.
workedExample: A classification endpoint can have 99.99% uptime while recall silently drops because the production population changed—system health alone would miss it.

visual.title: ML monitoring stack
visual.caption: Monitoring needs multiple layers because infrastructure can be healthy while the model or product outcome degrades.
